title: Medical Drone Telehealth Delivery in the Marshall Islands
summary: A medical drone successfully delivers a telehealth kit to a boat off the Kwajalein Atoll, proving it can bring more than medicine — a doctor no matter where the patient is.
body_markdown:
Off Kwajalein Atoll, a drone flies a telemedicine kit over open water, placing it directly aboard a vessel at sea.


### **A Telemedicine Clinic Delivered by Drone**


The payload was a satellite-linked


[VSee Telemedicine Kit](https://vsee.com/hardware#tm-kit) , designed to connect remote locations with off-site physicians.


The concept was simple. Beyond simply delivering medical supplies, could the drone transport the examination capability itself — effectively bringing an urgent care clinic over the water in less time?


Once aboard, could the telehealth kit establish a live link, even at sea? This was already proven once during a[boat ambulance pilot](https://vsee.com/blog/us-coast-guard-cadets-launch-sea-ambulance-telehealth-for-improved-veteran-access-to-healthcare/) with VSee, KALGOV, and US Coast Guard Academy cadets in 2024


### **Solving Remote Telehealth Challenges in Kwajalein Atoll**


This is the constant challenge of an atoll nation like the Republic of the Marshall Islands (RMI). It’s also the same problem rural and remote areas face: How to quickly reach medical care in disaster and emergency situations when time is of the essence and distance is a problem? The RMI is made up of over 1,100 little islands or islets; Kwajalein Atoll alone has approximately 100. Not every islet is inhabited and should be stationed with a telemedicine diagnostic kit.


Adding equipment to distant land locations doesn’t solve the access problem. I f there is an accident, medical care remains out of reach, and boat transit takes hours.


Flying the equipment directly to the patient inverts this challenge, testing whether real-time connectivity holds against wind, salt water, and moving vessels.

### **Disaster Response and Telehealth Joint Exercise**


This drone medical delivery flight was a disaster-response exercise with a team including Kwajalein’s disaster response coordinator Abon Arelong, the Hawaii National Guard, Kwajalein first responders, occurring in July 2025, organized by[Pacific Allies](https://www.usarpac.army.mil/Our-Story/Our-News/Article-Display/Article/3216885/pacific-allies-interns-address-climate-change-in-the-rmi/) to address climate change and national security in the RMI.


“By putting satellite-linked telehealth into the hands of the next generation of Marshallese leaders, VSee gives outer island communities access to healthcare that was unimaginable ten years ago.”


— Dr. Gregg Nakano, Executive Director, Pacific Allies


### **Future Medical Drone and Telehealth Demonstrations**


Following up on this 2025 medical delivery drone exercise, in August 2026, Pacific Allies and KALGOV conducted a[search-and-rescue demonstration](https://vsee.com/blog/telehealth-marshall-islands-drone-rescue/) in Kwajalein lagoon, using a drone to locate a “casualty” and then establish a three-clinician telehealth link. A casualty evacuation demonstration follows in July 2027, transitioning the drone payload from equipment to people.


With each milestone, the operational focus moves closer to directly serving the patient.
